unit_title: Unit 5: Cultural Heritages - Master Guide on Relative Clauses
content: Unit 5: Grammar Focus - Comprehensive Master Guide on Relative Clauses (Communicative English Skills II - EnLa102) ========================================= 1. CORE CONCEPTS AND FUNDAMENTALS OF RELATIVE CLAUSES ========================================= What is a Relative Clause? A Relative Clause (ደባይ ሀረግ/ዓረፍተ-ነገር) is a subordinate clause that modifies a noun or pronoun in the main clause. It acts like an adjective by giving essential or additional details about a person, object, place, time, or reason. Relative clauses are introduced by either Relative Pronouns or Relative Adverbs: • Relative Pronouns: who, whom, whose, which, that • Relative Adverbs: where, when, why Example: - Direct combination: I saw the girl. She lives near our campus. → I saw the girl who lives near our campus. ========================================= 2. EXHAUSTIVE BREAKDOWN OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS & ADVERBS ========================================= A. Relative Pronouns Matrix (Academic & Exam Standard) 1. WHO (Subject for Persons): • Exclusively refers to human subjects in formal academic grammar. • Subject role: The student who scored highest received an award. 2. WHOM (Object for Persons - Strict Exam Standard): • Exclusively refers to human objects in formal/academic English. • EXAM RULE: For all university exams, always select whom when referring to a person in the object position (e.g., The lecturer whom I met yesterday). • MANDATORY PREPOSITION RULE: Must be used directly after prepositions (e.g., to whom, with whom, about whom, for whom). • Example: Grace is the friend with whom he was in love. 3. WHOSE (Possessive for Persons, Animals, & Objects): • Shows possession or ownership (replaces his, her, its, their). • Example: There is a lucky person whose lottery ticket won 7,000,000 Birr. 4. WHICH (Subject / Object for Animals & Things, or Whole Clauses): • Refers to non-human subjects or objects. • Can also refer back to an entire preceding clause. • Example (Thing): His car, which cost 20,000 pounds, is broken. • Example (Whole clause): She passed me the salt, which fell on the floor. 5. THAT (Subject / Object for Persons, Animals, & Things): • Used ONLY in Defining Relative Clauses. • Replaces who or which in standard restrictive contexts. • STRICT RULE: That can NEVER be used after a comma or after a preposition! • Example: They wanted the picture that cost two pounds. ─────────────────────────── B. Relative Adverbs Matrix 1. WHERE (Place = Preposition + Which): • Modifies places (*in which, at which, on which*). • Example: This is a restaurant where you can find global cuisines. 2. WHEN (Time = Preposition + Which): • Modifies time references (*at which, in which, on which*). • Example: The moment when I found out the exam results was shocking. 3. WHY (Reason = For Which): • Modifies reasons (*for which*). • Example: I would like to know the reason why you decided not to join us. ========================================= 3. DEFINING VS. NON-DEFINING RELATIVE CLAUSES ========================================= A. Defining Relative Clauses (Essential Information) • Function: Contains indispensable information needed to identify the exact noun being discussed. • Commas: NO COMMAS ARE USED. • Use of 'That': That can freely replace who or which. • Omission: The relative pronoun CAN be omitted if it is the object of the clause. - Example 1: The man who sat next to me on the plane talked all the time. (Subject - Cannot omit) - Example 2: This is the shirt (that) I bought. (Object - Pronoun can be omitted: "This is the shirt I bought.") B. Non-Defining Relative Clauses (Extra / Parenthetical Information) • Function: Adds extra, non-essential background details. The main sentence remains complete without it. • Commas: MUST BE ENCLOSED IN COMMAS ( , ... , ). • Use of 'That': 'THAT' IS STRICTLY FORBIDDEN. You must use who, which, whom, or whose. • Omission: The relative pronoun CAN NEVER BE OMITTED. - Example 1: My father, who is 65 now, still works. - Example 2: Los Angeles, which is a popular tourist destination, is a fascinating city. ========================================= 4. OMISSION OF RELATIVE PRONOUNS (ZERO RELATIVE PRONOUN) ========================================= When are you allowed to drop who, whom, which, or that? 1. RULE 1 (Allowed): You can omit the relative pronoun ONLY when it functions as the OBJECT in a defining relative clause. • With Pronoun: The girl whom/that I met yesterday was helpful. • Omitted (Zero Pronoun): The girl [Ø] I met yesterday was helpful. 2. RULE 2 (Not Allowed - Subject Position): If the relative pronoun is the SUBJECT of the verb in the clause, it CANNOT be dropped. • Correct: I saw the girl who was outside our house. • Incorrect: I saw the girl was outside our house. ❌ 3. RULE 3 (Not Allowed - Non-Defining Clauses): You can NEVER drop relative pronouns in non-defining clauses (between commas). ========================================= 5. SOLVED TEXTBOOK ACTIVITIES (MODULE ANSWERS & EXPLANATIONS) ========================================= Activity 5.4 Solutions (Page 64-65): 1. This is a restaurant where you can find many different cuisines... *(Refers to place)* 2. The moment when I found out the exam results was one of the worst... *(Refers to time)* 3. Those who are eager to join the Spanish class should sign up... *(Human subject)* 4. Los Angeles, which is one of the most visited tourist destinations, is... *(Non-defining, thing/city)* 5. I would like to know the reason why you decided not to join us. *(Refers to reason)* 6. The Amazons, whose warrior nature is stressed in Greek mythology, have... *(Possessive)* 7. The Early Bronze Age was a period when / in which the climate was... *(Refers to time period)* 8. Anyone who is interested in mountaineering should have enough... *(Human subject)* 9. Creating a website which / that is accessible to color blind people... *(Defining, thing)* 10. One of the reasons why most of us change is because we need to adjust... *(Refers to reason)* 11. The 19th century artist, whose name I couldn't remember, was... *(Possessive name)* Activity 5.5 Solutions (Page 66): 1. Do you know anyone who can repair cigarette burns on clothes? *(Human subject)* 2. It's usually children from deprived backgrounds that / who cause the worst problems. 3. The Council provides bins in which waste paper can be deposited for recycling. *(Preposition 'in' requires 'which')* 4. Address the reference 'to whom it may concern', as it's very formal. *(Preposition 'to' requires 'whom')* 5. The town hall clock played a different tune at twelve every day, which amused the locals... *(Refers to whole preceding clause)* 6. There's a lucky person in this hall whose lottery ticket has just won them 7,000,000 Birr. 7. Why don't you tell the police what you told me yesterday? *(Nominal relative pronoun = 'the thing which')* 8. The film is set in the period when the divide between rich and poor was much greater... 9. You can put the photo wherever you think it looks best. Activity 5.6 & 5.7 Answers Summary (Page 67): • Activity 5.6: (1) that/which, (2) whose, (3) who/that, (4) who/that, (5) who/that, (6) that/which/omitted, (7) whom/that/omitted, (8) who/that, (9) who/that, (10) that/which. • Activity 5.7: Passage pronouns: (1) whose, (2) who/that, (3) which, (4) when, (5) which, (6) which/that. ========================================= 6. PITFALL CASES, EXAM TRICKS & COMMON ERRORS ========================================= TRICK 1: Using 'That' After a Comma (Non-Defining Trap) ❌ INCORRECT: Gondar, that is famous for its castles, is located in northern Ethiopia. ✅ CORRECT: Gondar, which is famous for its castles, is located in northern Ethiopia. 💡 EXAM TRICK: If you see a comma right before the blank space, NEVER choose that! TRICK 2: Preposition + 'That' or 'Who' Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The scholar to who I spoke yesterday gave a lecture. ❌ INCORRECT: The book about that we talked is in the library. ✅ CORRECT: The scholar to whom I spoke yesterday gave a lecture. ✅ CORRECT: The book about which we talked is in the library. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Directly after a preposition (to, with, about, in, for, on), you can ONLY use whom (for people) or which (for things)! TRICK 3: Human Object Trap ('Who' vs. 'Whom') ❌ INCORRECT (In Formal Exams): The candidate who we interviewed yesterday was selected. ✅ CORRECT (Formal Exam Standard): The candidate whom we interviewed yesterday was selected. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Identify if the human pronoun is a Subject or Object. "We interviewed him/her" → Object role $\rightarrow$ Use whom in exam questions! TRICK 4: The Double Pronoun / Repetition Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The cultural heritage that we preserved it last year is valuable. ✅ CORRECT: The cultural heritage that we preserved last year is valuable. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Relative pronouns replace personal pronouns (it, him, her, them). Do NOT keep the object pronoun inside the relative clause! TRICK 5: 'Where' vs 'Which' for Places Trap ❌ INCORRECT: This is the historical monument where I visited last week. ✅ CORRECT: This is the historical monument which/that I visited last week. ✅ CORRECT: This is the historical monument where I stayed last week. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Use where only if the place clause includes an implicit preposition of location (stayed at, lived in). If the place is a direct object of verbs like visit, buy, build, see, use which / that! TRICK 6: 'Whose' vs 'Who's' Contraction Trap ❌ INCORRECT: The researcher who's manuscript was published gave a lecture. ✅ CORRECT: The researcher whose manuscript was published gave a lecture. 💡 EXAM TRICK: Whose shows possession. Who's is a contraction for who is or who has. ========================================= 7. PRACTICE EXAM QUESTIONS & DETAILED RATIONALE ========================================= Question 1: The professor to ________ you sent the official application email has not responded yet. A. who B. whom C. that D. whose Correct Answer: B. whom Analysis / Rationale: The pronoun follows the preposition to and refers to a person (the professor) in the object position. In formal exam standard, only whom can follow a preposition for human objects. Question 2: Hawassa, ________ is known for its beautiful scenery and lake, attracts thousands of tourists annually. A. that B. where C. which D. what Correct Answer: C. which Analysis / Rationale: The clause is non-defining (enclosed in commas), which rules out that. Which is required because it functions as the subject for the verb is known. Question 3: Select the sentence where the relative pronoun CANNOT be omitted: A. The textbook that I borrowed from the university library was helpful. B. The tour guide whom we hired for the excursion was knowledgeable. C. The applicant who answered all technical questions correctly passed the interview. D. The traditional song which the cultural band performed was inspiring. Correct Answer: C. The applicant who answered all technical questions correctly passed the interview. Analysis / Rationale: In Option C, who acts as the SUBJECT of the clause verb answered, so it cannot be dropped. In options A, B, and D, the pronouns act as objects and can be omitted. Question 4: PITFALL QUESTION: The guest ________ speech inspired everyone at the cultural summit is a famous historian. A. who's B. whom C. whose D. who Correct Answer: C. whose Analysis / Rationale: The noun "speech" belongs to the guest (possessive relation). Option A (who's) is a trap meaning "who is" or "who has". Option C (whose) is the correct possessive relative pronoun. Question 5: PITFALL QUESTION: Is this the national museum ________ the government renovated last year? A. where B. which C. in where D. whose Correct Answer: B. which Analysis / Rationale: The verb renovated takes a direct object ("renovated the museum"). Because there is no preposition of location (such as at/in), which or that must be used instead of where.
